Nokalakevi (Archaeopolis)

A fortified city from the Lazic Wars above the Tekhuri river — walls, a secret tunnel and an active excavation.

Time needed
2 h
From Tbilisi
300 km · 4:30
Road
Paved
Car needed
Economy class
Season
All year
Entry
~10 ₾

Nokalakevi is one of the most important archaeological sites in western Georgia. Byzantine authors knew it as Archaeopolis, while Georgian tradition called it Tsikhegoji. It occupies a naturally defended position in the valley of the Tekhuri river and was a principal centre of the kingdom of Egrisi between the fourth and sixth centuries.

Its historical weight comes from the Lazic Wars, the sixth-century contest between Byzantium and Sasanian Persia for control of western Georgia. Nokalakevi was one of the key fortified nodes in that conflict, and the surviving walls reflect the military engineering of exactly that period.

What you will find on site:

  • The lower fortress walls and towers, partly consolidated and restored
  • A secret tunnel cut down through the rock to the Tekhuri, built to supply water during a siege
  • The remains of a basilica and a bath house
  • A small museum displaying finds from the excavations

A joint Georgian-British archaeological expedition has worked here for many years, so in summer you may well see active trenches and researchers at work. The climb to the upper fortress is steep and unshaded, but the view along the valley makes it worth the effort, and it clarifies exactly why the site was chosen.

Practical advice

Allow an hour and a half to two hours. Wear comfortable shoes: the ground is grassy and sloping, and the stairway down the water tunnel is narrow and damp, so a phone torch helps. Summers here are hot and humid, which makes a morning visit far more pleasant than midday, and you should carry water. Park on the small area by the entrance. The nearest cafes and ATM are in Senaki, so take cash with you before you arrive.

How to get there from Tbilisi

Nokalakevi is about 300 km and four and a half hours from Tbilisi. Follow the E60 west through Khashuri, the Rikoti section, Kutaisi and Samtredia, then turn toward Senaki and continue a few kilometres north to the site. The whole route is paved; the final stretch is a narrow village road but in sound condition, so an economy car is sufficient. Fill up in Samtredia or Senaki. The site combines well with Martvili Canyon in a single day, since both lie within about forty minutes of each other.
